source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs played a 2-4-6 style rule discovery game (propose a triple, get yes/no, guess the rule). Models show confirmation bias: they often test triples that fit their current guess. Bias is measured as I:C, the ratio of incompatible (could falsify) to compatible tests.
numbers: Task success ranged 6% to 78% across models within a 45-turn cap. Success correlates positively with I:C (more disconfirming tests, more success), significant for thinking and non-thinking models, stronger for thinking models.
quote: LLMs exhibit confirmation bias, often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it.
limits: Max 45 turns; synthetic rule set where the first triple fits several rules; Qwen3, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, QwQ, R1-distill. Correlation, not proof of cause.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that testing against your own hypothesis predicts success in an LLM. The schema can count the share of disconfirming tests in code.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, baseline results table
finding: Baseline success per model on the rule game. Thinking mode beats non-thinking mode for the Qwen3 sizes, but the gain is not matched by a consistent rise in I:C, so thinking helps by other means too.
numbers: Non-thinking baseline success: Qwen3-8B 0.06, Qwen3-14B 0.23, Qwen3-32B 0.33, Llama-3.3-70B 0.21, GPT-4o 0.11. Gemini-2.5-Pro (thinking) baseline 0.73.
limits: Table text is garbled in PDF extraction; thinking-mode columns for Qwen3 were not read cleanly, so only the clean cells are given.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of GPT-4o is poor on this paradigm; a scaffold has large headroom.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, Think-in-Opposites and Dual-Goal prompts
finding: Two human debiasing prompts were tested. Think-in-Opposites (TiO): pick one property of the last test triple and build a triple opposite in that property. Dual-Goal: the model states two rules (DAX = hidden rule, MED = its complement) and feedback is DAX/MED instead of yes/no.
numbers: TiO improved task success in all 11 model-setting cases; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Both raised I:C in 18 of 22 cases. Abstract: average discovery rate 42% to 56%. Examples: Llama-3.3-70B 0.21 to 0.38 with TiO; GPT-4o 0.11 to 0.16 (TiO) and 0.14 (Dual-Goal); Qwen3-32B thinking I:C 0.14 to 0.54 with TiO.
quote: Prompting LLMs with such instruction consistently decreases confirmation bias in LLMs
limits: Significant for thinking models; mixed for non-thinking models. Dual-Goal hurt Qwen3-14B non-thinking (0.23 to 0.13) and Qwen3-32B non-thinking (0.33 to 0.10).
agent_relevance: A forced opposite-test instruction is a cheap operator, but it works reliably only when the model can reason first. Check effect before using it on weak calls.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, distillation and Blicket transfer
finding: They fine-tuned models on TiO traces with high success and high I:C, then tested on a different task, the Blicket detector (which objects switch a machine on).
numbers: Blicket baseline: Qwen3-8B 0.32, Qwen3-32B 0.57; with TiO prompt 0.40 and 0.86. Wason-distilled 8B student 0.34 (small gain), below prompting. I:C correlated with success in Blicket too (about 0.65 non-thinking, 0.74 thinking, from figure labels).
limits: Transfer gain is small and below prompting; 192 Blicket episodes per cell.
agent_relevance: A task-agnostic falsification habit helps a little, but scaffold-time prompting beat weight-time transfer here.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: WILT turns the 2-4-6 task into a benchmark: hidden rule over three numbers, up to 30 tests, then one guess as a Python lambda. LLMs struggle; a common failure is confirmation bias, stronger models try to falsify.
numbers: 50 hidden rules. Accuracy: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50, o1-mini 13/50, o1-preview 12/50, chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50, Mistral Large 2 11/50, GPT-4o 9/50, Llama 3.1 405B 8/50, GPT-4o-mini 6/50, Claude 3 Haiku 1/50. Best model 28%.
quote: we find a common failure mode to be confirmation bias
limits: 50 rules; each rule in fresh context; workshop paper; rules are simple booleans.
agent_relevance: Single-turn reasoning strength (o1) did not win; multi-turn evidence gathering did. A scaffold should manage the test budget in code.

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT, repeated tests and hypothesis-space reduction
finding: Models often repeat tests they already ran, sometimes dozens of times, and propose useless tests. The authors estimate how many of 2000 random candidate rules each test crosses off.
numbers: Average repeated tests per rule: GPT-4o-mini 9.78, GPT-4o 2.84, Llama 3.1 70B 2.16, o1-preview 0.06, chatgpt-4o-latest 0.06. Average guesses used: GPT-4o-mini 27.2, GPT-4o 26.6, o1-preview 12.1.
limits: The 2000 random lambdas are a proxy for the true hypothesis space.
agent_relevance: Program-side dedup of tests and a count of eliminated hypotheses is easy and useful (G5: code counts).

source: Banatt et al. (2024) WILT, evidence gathering versus rule inference split
finding: They separated evidence gathering from rule inference: one model got the stripped test results made by another model and had to give the rule in one turn.
numbers: o1-mini given tests produced by chatgpt-4o-latest guessed 19 of 50 rules, above the best single-model full run (14/50). Claude 3.5 Sonnet degraded more than others when its own reasoning was stripped from its tests.
limits: One highlighted pairing; N is 50 rules.
agent_relevance: A split where one process proposes tests and a stronger reasoner infers the rule beat any single model. Note G4: roles from one model are not independent.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: Evaluating Inductive Reasoning in LLMs with Rule Discovery Games
finding: Wason-style game on semantic categories (WordNet), 12 LLMs, 100 games each. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones; negative testing is the main driver of success. When the hypothesis is narrower than the truth, only tests outside the hypothesis can falsify it.
numbers: Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Spearman of positive-test share with success: rho = -0.779 (p=0.003).
limits: One paper; taxonomic rules, not numbers; each model is also its own oracle (oracle accuracy 85-95%).
agent_relevance: Reproduces the human 2-4-6 effect in a new domain and gives a clean rule: when your guess is the narrower set, test outside it.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench, falsification rates and failure patterns
finding: Each test turn is labelled by the set relation between hypothesis H and truth R. H narrower than R held in over 50% of turns for almost every model. Reasoning models more often produced a test that truly falsified a wrong hypothesis.
numbers: Conclusive falsification rate: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%; lowest Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%, GPT-5-Nano 26.6%. Positive-test share: GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2% versus 66-82% for instruction-tuned. Positive share against falsification rate rho = -0.937 (p<0.001).
limits: Failed games also drift into disjoint or partly overlapping hypotheses, so confirmation is not the whole story; oracle quality alone did not explain success.
agent_relevance: The falsification rate is a per-turn signal code can compute. Failure also comes from bad hypothesis paths.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench, bias in successful versus failed games
finding: Within the same model, failed games show more confirmation testing than successful ones.
numbers: GPT-5.2-Chat positive-test share 20% in successful games versus 50% in failed; GPT-OSS-20B 17% versus 53%.
limits: Appendix split by outcome; no causal test.
agent_relevance: A stale-run signal (many positive tests in a row) could trigger a forced outside-the-hypothesis test (G1 style, on a signal).

source: Dasgupta, Lampinen, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models, like humans, show content effects on reasoning tasks (PNAS Nexus; arXiv 2207.07051)
finding: Chinchilla, PaLM 2 and GPT-3.5 solve the Wason task better with realistic content than arbitrary or nonsense content, as humans do. Humans were near chance overall.
numbers: Realistic-content advantage significant for humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 (all z > 2.2, p < 0.03); only marginal (z about 1.78, p about 0.08) for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2. Slowest 15% of humans (over 80 s) were above chance only on realistic rules.
limits: Generated problems, forced two-card choice, DC-PMI likelihood scoring (raw scoring kept the content effects). 2022-2023 era models.
agent_relevance: Content shapes accuracy more than logical form. Restating an abstract rule in concrete terms may help, if a check confirms the meaning is unchanged.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2024) content effects, answer patterns
finding: Humans show matching bias (choose the cards named in the rule) and often pick both cards of one rule part. Models give more correct responses than humans, and their error patterns differ from human ones.
numbers: Humans: at or below chance in all conditions for the fast majority. Two larger models above chance on arbitrary rules. A bonus-payment second sample did not change results.
limits: Pattern analysis by multinomial regression in the appendix; online human participants.
agent_relevance: Fluent models do not copy human errors one to one, so human bias lists should not be assumed to transfer.

source: Seals and Shalin (2024) Evaluating the Deductive Competence of Large Language Models (NAACL; arXiv 2309.05452)
finding: Seven-billion-scale open models (Guanaco, MPT, BLOOM, Falcon, plus Llama-2, Wizard) mostly fail the Wason task in its usual form. Changing format and content does not fix overall performance.
numbers: Chance 1/6. Realistic over shuffled rules: OR 1.30 [1.05-1.62]; social-rule by content interaction OR 1.59; switched social rules worse than standard social rules (as in humans). LLMs solved social-rule problems about 30% of the time versus about 70% for humans. Per-model accuracies mostly 0.06-0.29.
limits: Small open models of 2023; option-likelihood scoring, not free generation.
agent_relevance: Social framing helps small models much less than humans; do not count on it alone.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of Deontic Conditional Reasoning in LLMs: The Case of Wason's Selection Task
finding: 160 problems (80 deontic, 80 descriptive; 20 per negation pattern). Nine open models, zero-shot, few-shot and chain of thought. Every model is more accurate on deontic than descriptive rules, by 5.0 to 45 points.
numbers: Zero-shot deontic accuracy: gpt-oss-120b 100.0 (+30 over descriptive), qwen3-32b 98.8 (+38.8), qwen3-14b 97.5 (+45), gpt-oss-20b 67.5 (+27.5), gemma3-27b 77.5, llama-3.3-70b 62.5, gemma3-12b 58.8, gemma3-4b 17.5. Few-shot gpt-oss-20b 91.2.
limits: Exact-match scoring (must pick exactly the right set); open-weight models only.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models reach near ceiling on deontic Wason; the abstract descriptive form stays the hard one.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Deontic Wason, matching bias versus confirmation bias
finding: With negated rule parts, a confirmation-bias model should pick true antecedent and true consequent. A matching-bias model picks cards named in the rule. Model errors fit matching bias better.
numbers: gpt-oss-20b zero-shot, deontic: for p->q picks true antecedent 100%, true consequent 45%, false consequent 55%; for p->not-q picks false consequent 95%, true consequent 5%.
limits: Percentages over 20 problems per polarity; one model shown in the main text.
agent_relevance: The 'confirmation bias' label for Wason errors may be wrong for models; lexical matching is a rival cause. Vary rule wording to check.

source: Alsagheer, Karanjai, Shi (2024) Comparing Rationality Between Large Language Models and Humans
finding: ChatGPT gave wrong answers across the Wason items and its explanations showed misunderstanding, while some humans did better.
numbers: Reported ChatGPT Wason total score 0.5 (scale unclear); low-scoring humans 4% to 15%; about 350 ChatGPT API calls; 50 online human questionnaires.
limits: Weak paper: scoring unclear, model version not stated, text partly inconsistent. Low reliability.
agent_relevance: Shows how early ChatGPT-era claims can mislead; do not rely on it.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in LLMs, as reported in a UCL press release
finding: Seven LLMs on classic cognitive tests including Wason. Models were irrational in ways different from humans and inconsistent between runs.
numbers: Press report: Wason correct answers from 90% for GPT-4 to 0% for GPT-3.5 and Google Bard; Llama 2 70b 10%.
limits: Secondary source seen only in search results; the paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: GPT-4-class models solved the basic letter-card task when asked directly; weak models failed it.

source: Huang, Jin, Li, Li, Candes, Leskovec (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: An LLM agent loop built on Popper's falsification. One agent proposes a measurable implication of a hypothesis as a null test, another runs it with code, p-values become e-values and are combined by sequential testing that controls Type-I error. This is a hypothesis-testing method already inside an agent loop.
numbers: Type-I target 0.1. Power: POPPER 0.610 (DiscoveryBench), 0.897 (TargetVal-IL2), 0.717 (TargetVal-IFNG) versus ReAct 0.378, 0.140, 0.040. Abstract text: 66.5% more power than ReAct on DiscoveryBench; 3.17x Self-Refine on IL2.
limits: Six domains; negatives made by column permutation; baselines without statistical control inflated errors; power valid only for methods with error control.
agent_relevance: Template: a code-run statistical gate decides rejection; the model only designs the test.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER versus human experts and across model sizes
finding: Nine computational biologists did the same validation tasks. POPPER matched their Type-I error and power (no significant difference) and was much faster. Model strength mattered.
numbers: POPPER 9.7x faster, 3.6x more lines of code, 2.5x more statistical tests. Claude Haiku 3.5 had high Type-I error; Llama 3.3 70B, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 3.5 and o1 kept reasonable error control. Removing the relevance checker raised Type-I error.
limits: Nine experts; one benchmark (TargetVal-IL2) for the human comparison.
agent_relevance: Weak models need the statistical gate and a relevance check even more.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning (NeurIPS)
finding: Hypotheses are kept as natural-language rules; an LLM proposes and updates them inside a Monte Carlo belief update, and the next experiment is chosen by an information criterion. This is optimal data selection in the Oaksford and Chater spirit, built on an LLM.
numbers: Zendo score out of 8: human 5.26, direct LLM (ReAct-style) 4.60, online fuzzy 6.01 or 6.18, batch hard 6.55. ActiveACRE task solving: online hard 0.35 versus batch hard 0.15 and refinement 0.10 (table cells partly garbled). Human-data log-likelihood: online fuzzy -1478.8, online hard -5209.9.
limits: Hard-rule model is most accurate but fuzzy online model best fits human behaviour; table layout garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Online belief updates over several live rules beat a one-shot or refine-only loop. Keep many hypotheses, not one.

source: Choudhury, Williamson, Golinski, Miao, Bickford Smith, Kirchhof, Zhang, Rainforth (2026) BED-LLM (ICLR)
finding: At each turn, pick the question with the highest expected information gain over candidate hypotheses (using LLM probabilities), then update. Compared with plain prompting for questions.
numbers: On average success on 20 Questions up 37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; more than doubled in over half the setups and never decreased.
limits: Entropy-only scoring was the strongest alternative; it confuses noise with information (high entropy, zero information gain). 20 Questions has a closed hypothesis set.
agent_relevance: Code-side choice of the most discriminating test is the machine form of Oaksford and Chater. Fits a test-selection operator.

source: Grand, Pepe, Tenenbaum, Andreas (2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later? Building Rational Agents that Explore and Act Like People (ICLR)
finding: In a Battleship dialogue game (N=42 humans), many LLMs ask uninformative questions. Sampling plus expected-information-gain scoring raised question value a lot.
numbers: Captain EIG up by as much as 0.227 bits (94.2% of ceiling). Llama-4-Scout win rate 8% to 82%, beating humans and GPT-5 (0% to 67% against GPT-5) at about 1% of GPT-5 cost. Spotter accuracy up to +14.7 points (Claude 4 Opus 86.8 to 94.4; GPT-4.1 75.2 to 90.9). Zero-information questions: Llama-4-Scout 18.5%, GPT-4o 14.6%. Guess Who? replication +42.4 points for Llama-4-Scout.
limits: Game with a computable ground truth; needs a program that can simulate answers.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a code layer scoring candidate tests by information gain lifts weak models above frontier ones.

source: Gandhi, Li, et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Progress in Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: Ten environments built as generative models; experiment value scored by expected information gain. LLM agents (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen, OpenThinker) struggle at design and model discovery; adding explicit statistical modelling (Box's Apprentice) did not significantly help.
numbers: 32B models beat 7B ones; closed models generally beat open ones. No single headline number in the abstract.
limits: Benchmark paper; detailed EIG regret numbers not extracted by me.
agent_relevance: Experiment design stays a weak spot even with tools; an external scorer is needed.

source: Link across Piriyakulkij (2024), Choudhury (2026) and Grand (2026): Oaksford and Chater optimal data selection as the machine template
finding: All three machine papers choose the next test by expected information gain over a set of hypotheses, which is the idea of Oaksford and Chater's 1994 account of the Wason task, now run by code with an LLM supplying hypotheses and likelihoods.
numbers: No new numbers; combines the gains listed in the lines above (+37.4 points on 20 Questions, +0.227 bits on Battleship).
limits: Link drawn by this agent from the papers read; the 1994 paper was not opened in this angle.
agent_relevance: The method family is already engineered. Reuse EIG scoring for the test-selection operator rather than invent a new rule.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Deontic Wason, prompt effects (zero-shot, few-shot, chain of thought)
finding: Prompt style changed accuracy a lot, and not always upward. Few-shot examples helped most non-reasoning models. Zero-shot chain of thought helped some and hurt others.
numbers: Deontic accuracy zero/few/CoT: gemma3-12b 58.8 / 78.7 / 43.8; gemma3-4b 17.5 / 21.2 / 38.8; gemma3-27b 77.5 / 76.2 / 62.5; llama-3.3-70b 62.5 / 78.7 / 83.8. Chain of thought was not run for the reasoning models (n/a).
limits: One rule type, 80 deontic problems, exact-match scoring, open models only.
agent_relevance: A fixed 'think step by step' operator is not safe across models. Measure it per model before putting it in the scaffold.
